Social Security modification: federally taxable benefits are fully exempt only if the taxpayer has reached full Social Security retirement age (66 to 67 depending on birth year) and federal AGI is at or below the 2026 threshold. approximations: H.4216 (Act 110 of 2026) restructures SC tax retroactive to January 1, 2026. Federal AGI is now the starting point, and federal standard and itemized deductions are gone. The statutory rates are 1.99% on SC taxable income up to $30,000 and 5.21% above (the same thresholds for every filing status). All other state deductions, exemptions and credits are retained, including the retirement, age-65, military-retirement and Social Security subtractions and the dependent exemption.

The new SC Income Adjusted Deduction (SCIAD) is folded into the brackets, so standardDeduction is 0. SCIAD is $15,000 single / $30,000 joint ($22,500 head of household) and phases out linearly between federal AGI $40,000 and $95,000 (single) or $80,000 and $190,000 (joint). The brackets reproduce exactly 'income minus SCIAD, then 1.99%/5.21%'. Inside the phase-out range the marginal rate is 5.21% x 14/11 = 6.63%. The one approximation is that SCIAD is keyed to federal AGI, while these brackets apply after the retirement and 65+ deductions, so the phase-out window lands up to that deduction amount higher in AGI terms than it should.
Retirement deduction, per person, on qualified retirement income (pensions, IRA, 401(k), government plans): $3,000 under age 65, $10,000 at 65+.

Age-65 deduction: $15,000 per person aged 65+ against any income, reduced by any retirement deduction claimed. Modeled as extraDeduction65 = $5,000 on top of the $10,000 retirement deduction. That is exact when the person has at least $10,000 of retirement income. Someone 65+ with less retirement income really gets the full $15,000 against other income, which this record understates.
Military retirement is fully deductible at any age (since 2022). Federal, state and local civilian pensions get only the retirement and 65+ deductions, so govPensionExempt is false.
Further top-rate cuts toward 1.99% are triggered only when revenue grows 5% or more. None applies to 2026. The nonrefundable SC EITC is capped at $200 under H.4216 (not modeled).

approximations: The statutory rate is a flat 4.45% for 2026 (SB 60, 2026 session, down from 4.5%). The brackets fold in the nonrefundable taxpayer tax credit and its phase-out, so they are not a statutory schedule.

Taxpayer credit: 6% of the federal standard deduction (2026: $16,100 single / $32,200 joint, giving $966 / $1,932), reduced by 1.3% of Utah taxable income above a base amount ($18,213 single / $36,426 joint in 2025). Tax = max(0, 4.45% x income - credit). Algebraically that equals 0% up to $20,918, 5.75% (4.45% + 1.3%) until the credit is gone at $92,521, then 4.45% (joint: $41,835 / $185,041). This is exact for a filer taking the federal standard deduction.

Not captured in the brackets: the federal additional standard deduction for age 65+ (2026: $2,050 single, $1,650 per spouse) raises the credit by $123 / $99 per person and extends the phase-out. Itemizers and filers with dependents get a larger credit. The OBBBA $6,000 senior deduction isn't part of the federal standard deduction and doesn't enter the Utah credit.

Social Security credit: 4.45% of federally taxable benefits, reduced by $0.25 per $1 of income above $54,000 single / $90,000 joint ($45,000 married filing separately). Since 2025 (SB 71) the income test uses Utah taxable income rather than federal AGI. The record treats Social Security as fully exempt at or below the threshold and fully taxed above it. In reality the credit tapers over the 4 x credit amount above the threshold (for example about $3,600 for a $20,000 taxable benefit), so tax is overstated just above the threshold.
Retirement tax credit: $450 per person, only for those born on or before 1952, and not combinable with the Social Security credit. Ignored (retirementExclusion null).

Military retirement credit = 4.45% x taxable military retirement pay, which makes it effectively fully exempt (it can be combined with the Social Security credit). Federal, state and local civilian pensions, IRA and 401(k) distributions are fully taxable.
